links.outcome: Diagnosis acceptance after algorithm adaptations informed by logged rejections and interviews
links.effect: Rejections were logged (acceptance 94.1% Tanzania vs 67.2% Rwanda for 2 months–14 years); adaptations based on rejection reasons improved acceptance for some diagnoses.
links.quote: A before–after analysis showed improved acceptance for some diagnoses following adaptations.

links.outcome: Clinician acceptance of proposed diagnoses after feedback-informed algorithm adaptations
links.effect: Acceptance improved for some diagnoses after adaptations informed by clinician feedback and expert input; numerical before–after effects were not reported.
links.quote: A before–after analysis showed improved acceptance for some diagnoses following adaptations.

links.effect: Logging diagnosis acceptance and rejection combined with qualitative feedback provided useful insights into clinical content acceptance.
links.quote: Allowing healthcare providers to accept or reject diagnoses proposed by digital CDSAs, combined with qualitative feedback to explore reasons for rejection, provides useful insights into the acceptance of clinical content and should be considered by other CDSAs to inform approaches to address and improve acceptability.

links.effect: Adapting algorithms based on findings from overridden or rejected diagnoses led to improved acceptance for some diagnoses.
links.quote: A before–after analysis showed improved acceptance for some diagnoses following adaptations.

screen.practice: clinician accept/reject of proposed diagnoses with feedback-driven algorithm adaptation
screen.reason: Evaluates a real-world primary care deployment of the ePOCT+ clinical decision support algorithm in Tanzania and Rwanda, assessing clinician acceptance and testing the impact of algorithm adaptations based on user feedback via a before-after analysis.
